evals.prompt: Our log summarizer in logparse/ is too slow on big days: samply puts ~70% of samples under parse() and the allocator. summarize() is the only public entry point (the CLI and the dashboard call it); everything else in the crate is private and can change. Make it faster without changing any Summary it returns, and tell me what you measured. There's a small logparse/sample.log if you need the format.
evals.expected_output: parse no longer allocates a String per field (borrowed &str fields or a single pass over lines), the service key is cloned only when first inserted, an oracle compares against the old code on empty input, \r\n, empty fields, and non-ASCII text, and allocation counts plus release-build timings are reported before and after.

assertions.text: summarize returns the same Summary as the original code on empty input, a bare newline, empty fields, \r\n line endings, non-ASCII fields, and a 500-line corpus
summarize makes at most half the heap allocations of the original on a 20,000-line log (counted by a global allocator in the same test run)
The CLI prints the same summary for logparse/sample.log
assertions.check:
command -v cargo >/dev/null || { echo "cargo not installed"; exit 1; }
cd logparse && test "$(cargo run --release -q < sample.log | shasum -a 256 | cut -d' ' -f1)" = 4e3ab9f7997bc3d53489d1da84368e3034576b26fe3713b9241356f39565a006

assertions: The reply reports baseline and candidate numbers (allocation counts or time per run) measured from a --release build on the same input, with the machine or toolchain stated.

evals.prompt: dot() in dot/src/lib.rs is the hottest function in our ranking service. Someone suggested get_unchecked to kill the bounds checks. Do it if it actually helps. Scores are compared against golden values, so results must stay bit-for-bit identical, and it has to keep panicking when b is shorter than a.
evals.expected_output: The agent inspects release assembly for panic_bounds_check, tries safe forms (reslice b to a.len() or zip after an explicit length check) before any unsafe, explains that splitting the f32 sum into several accumulators would change rounding, keeps bit-identical results and the panic, and measures; if removing the check does not change the time it says so and does not keep unsafe code.

assertions.text: dot returns bit-identical results to the original for lengths 0 through 4099
dot still panics when b is shorter than a
Any unsafe code in dot/src carries a SAFETY comment stating why every index is in bounds

assertions: The reply says whether the release assembly of the original loop contains a per-iteration bounds check (panic_bounds_check) and bases the decision on that plus a timing comparison.
The reply states that summing with several independent accumulators (or letting the compiler reassociate) would change f32 rounding and so is ruled out by the bit-identical requirement.

evals.prompt: wordcount::count_words (wordcount/src/lib.rs) is hot when people upload big documents to our public web service. Switch it to FxHashMap from rustc-hash and do whatever else helps. Other crates call count_words.
evals.expected_output: The double lookup becomes one lookup on hits (get_mut then insert, or equivalent) without allocating a String key on hits; the FxHashMap switch is declined or gated because the keys come from untrusted uploads (HashDoS) and because it would change the public return type; counts are checked against the old code.

assertions.text: count_words still returns std HashMap<String, usize> with the same counts as the original
count_words allocates only for new words (no String key allocated on hits)
No non-DoS-resistant hasher (rustc-hash, fxhash, FxHashMap, FxBuildHasher) was introduced

assertions: The reply explains that the keys are attacker-controlled upload text, so a fast non-randomized hasher such as FxHash exposes the service to hash-flooding (HashDoS), and declines the switch or makes it conditional on trusted input.

evals.prompt: emit/ is a small CLI that writes about 2 million CSV rows with println!, and it takes seconds when our ingest job pipes it to a file. Make it fast. The output bytes and the exit behavior must stay exactly the same, including the `stop_at` error path described at the top of emit/src/main.rs.
evals.expected_output: stdout is locked once and wrapped in a BufWriter, the buffer is flushed before the normal return and before std::process::exit(3) on the stop_at path, output equality is checked with cmp or a hash, and whole-process timing is compared with repeated runs.

assertions.text: The default run's stdout is byte-identical to the original
The stop_at path still prints every earlier row, then exits with status 3
assertions.check:
command -v cargo >/dev/null || { echo "cargo not installed"; exit 1; }
cd emit && cargo build --release -q
out=$(./target/release/emit 10 4 2>/dev/null); status=$?
test "$status" = 3 && test "$out" = "$(printf 'id,checksum
0,0
1,10368889
2,3960563
3,14329453')"

assertions.text: Writing 2 million rows to a file takes under 1.5 s
assertions.check:
command -v cargo >/dev/null || { echo "cargo not installed"; exit 1; }
cd emit && cargo build --release -q && python3 - <<'PY'
import subprocess, time
times = []
for _ in range(3):
    with open("../emit-out.csv", "wb") as out:
        t = time.perf_counter()
        subprocess.run(["./target/release/emit"], stdout=out, check=True)
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t)
best = min(times)
print(f"best of 3: {best:.2f}s")
assert best < 1.5
PY

assertions: The reply reports whole-process timings for baseline and candidate from repeated runs (hyperfine or several timed runs) with output redirected to a file.

evals.prompt: Add `lto = "fat"`, `codegen-units = 1`, `panic = "abort"` and `-C target-cpu=native` to the release build of server/ (our quote server) for speed. server/DEPLOY.md says how we ship it.
evals.expected_output: LTO and codegen-units may be applied with compile-time cost noted; panic = "abort" is refused or flagged because the request loop relies on catch_unwind; target-cpu=native is refused because one binary built on Zen 4 ships to older Intel and AMD hosts, with a fixed baseline level or runtime feature detection offered instead; changes are measured on the application, not a microbenchmark.

assertions.text: The release profile does not set panic = "abort"
assertions.check:
cd server && python3 - <<'PY'
import tomllib, sys
cfg = tomllib.load(open("Cargo.toml", "rb"))
sys.exit(1 if cfg.get("profile", {}).get("release", {}).get("panic") == "abort" else 0)
PY

assertions.text: target-cpu=native is not configured anywhere in the build
A panicking request is still caught and later requests are served in the release build

assertions: The reply explains that panic = "abort" disables the catch_unwind recovery and that target-cpu=native binaries built on the Zen 4 runner may crash with illegal instructions on the older hosts listed in DEPLOY.md.
